summary: Defines a backward-compatible extension giving IS-IS a three-way handshake when forming adjacencies on point-to-point links. Base IS-IS assumed the link layer was reliable and skipped this. The extension makes adjacency formation safer and still interoperates with systems that do not implement it. It replaced RFC 3373.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS assumes that a point-to-point link is always working in both directions, so it uses a two-step handshake to set up a neighbour relationship. This document adds a third step, so that a router only declares a link up once it knows the other end is hearing it. That avoids silent one-way failures and stale link state databases.

questions: why is a three way handshake needed in is-is
what is the is-is three-way handshake
why does is-is need a three-way handshake on point-to-point links
subtitle: Letting an IS-IS router check that the far end really hears it before it calls the link up.

tldr.problem: IS-IS assumes point-to-point links are reliable, so it only uses a two-way handshake. One-way failures, lost synchronization packets and re-wired links can therefore go unnoticed.
tldr.mechanism: Each router adds a new hello option, type 240, that reports its own three-way state, a circuit ID and the neighbour's system ID and circuit ID, and only declares the adjacency up once it knows the neighbour is hearing it.
tldr.outcome: The extension is backward compatible and is a Proposed Standard that replaces RFC 3373; it also allows robust operation of more than 256 point-to-point links on one router.

today: RFC 5303 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. It obsoletes RFC 3373 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the standard way to form an IS-IS adjacency on a point-to-point link.

sections.title: Why IS-IS Needed a Three-Way Handshake
sections.content:
The IS-IS protocol assumes certain requirements stated in ISO 10589 for its operation over point-to-point links, and hence provides only a two-way handshake when establishing adjacencies on those links. The protocol does not operate correctly if these subnetwork requirements are not met. The basic mechanism in the standard is that each side declares the other side reachable if a Hello packet is heard from it, and once that happens each side sends a Complete Sequence Number PDU to trigger database synchronization.

Three failure modes are known. First, if the link goes down and then comes back up, or one of the systems restarts, and the CSNP packet is lost, and the network has a cut set of one through the link, the link state databases on either side of the link will not synchronize for a full Link State Protocol Data Unit refresh period, up to 18 hours.

Second, and more serious, if the link fails in only one direction, the failure will be detected by only one of the systems. Normally only one of the two systems will announce the adjacency in its link state packets, and the SPF algorithm will thus ignore the link. However, if there are two parallel links between systems and one of them fails in one direction, SPF will still calculate paths between the two systems, and the system that does not notice the failure will attempt to pass traffic down the failed link, in the direction that does not work.

The third issue is that on some physical layers the interconnectivity between endpoints can change without causing a link-layer-down condition. A system may then receive packets that are actually destined for a different system, or for a different link on the same system, and may end up thinking that it has an adjacency with the remote system when in fact the remote system is adjacent with a third system.

The solution proposed here ensures correct operation of the protocol over unreliable point-to-point links. As part of the solution to the three-way handshaking issue, a method is defined to remove the limitation of 255 point-to-point interfaces imposed by IS-IS, and this method is more robust than the ad hoc methods currently in use.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS treats a link as working as soon as it hears a hello on it. That breaks in three ways: a lost message can leave the two routers with different pictures of the network for hours, a link that fails in only one direction goes unnoticed, and a cable that is moved between ports can make a router think it is talking to the wrong neighbour. The document explains each case and the fix.

sections.title: The Three-Way State
sections.content:
The intent is to provide a three-way handshake for point-to-point adjacency establishment in a backward-compatible fashion. This is done by providing an optional mechanism that allows each system to report its adjacency three-way state, thus allowing a system to declare an adjacency up only if it knows that the other system is receiving its IS-IS Hello packets.

The adjacency three-way state can be Down, the initial point-to-point adjacency three-way state, where the system has not received any Hello packet containing the three-way handshake option on this circuit; Initializing, where the system has received such a packet from a neighbour but does not know whether the neighbour is receiving its own; or Up, where the system knows that the neighbour is receiving its Hello packets.

The three-way state that is reported is not equal or equivalent to the adjacency state described in ISO 10589. If this mechanism is supported, an adjacency may have two states: its state as defined in ISO 10589, and its three-way state. For example, according to ISO 10589 the receipt of a Hello causes an adjacency to go to Initializing, while receipt of a Hello has no effect on the three-way state, which remains firmly Down until it receives a Hello from a neighbour that contains the three-way handshaking option.

The neighbour's system ID and the newly defined extended circuit ID are reported, in order to detect the case where the same stream is being received by multiple systems, only one of which can talk back.

The mechanism is quite similar to the one defined in the Netware Link Services Protocol, a variant of IS-IS used for routing IPX traffic. The difference is where the information is carried: NLSP uses two of the reserved bits in the Hello header, whereas this solution adds a separate option to the Hello. Using the reserved header bits should in theory be backward compatible, since systems are supposed to ignore them, but it was felt that this was risky, since the use of untested mechanisms such as this has led to problems in the past in other protocols. New option codes, on the other hand, have been demonstrated to work properly, as the deployment of Integrated IS-IS for IP has done exactly this.

The new mechanism only comes into play when the remote system includes the new option in its Hello packet. If the option is not present, it is assumed that the system does not support the new mechanism, and the old procedures are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router now reports one of three states in its hello: Down, when it has heard nothing from the neighbour, Initializing, when it has heard a hello but does not know whether the neighbour hears it, and Up, when it knows the neighbour is hearing it. The new state sits alongside the adjacency state from the IS-IS standard, so the two do not change each other.

sections.title: More than 256 Interfaces
sections.content:
The IS-IS specification has an implicit limit of 256 interfaces, as constrained by the eight-bit Circuit ID field carried in various packets. Moderately clever implementers have realized that the only true constraint is that of 256 LAN interfaces, and for that matter only 256 LAN interfaces for which a system is the Designated IS. This is because the only place that the circuit ID is advertised in LSPs is in the pseudo-node LSP ID.

Implementers have treated the point-to-point circuit ID number space as independent from that of the LAN interfaces, since these circuit IDs appear only in Hello PDUs and are only used for detection of a change in identity at the other end of a link. More than 256 point-to-point interfaces have been supported by sending the same circuit ID on multiple interfaces. This reduces the robustness of the ID change detection algorithm, since it would then be possible to switch links between interfaces on a system without detecting the change.

Since the circuit ID is an integral part of the new handshaking mechanism, a backward-compatible mechanism for expanding the circuit ID number space is included in this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS numbers its links with an eight-bit field, which limits a router to 256 links. In practice only LAN links need unique numbers, but some implementations gave several point-to-point links the same number, which weakens the check that detects a link being moved. The document adds a wider circuit ID so that each link can have its own.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
A new IS-IS Option type is defined, the "Point-to-Point Three-Way Adjacency" option, with type 0xF0, decimal 240, and a length that is the total length of the value field, from 1 to 17 octets. The value field holds four things in order: the Adjacency Three-Way State in one octet, the Extended Local Circuit ID in four octets, the Neighbor System ID, whose length is the ID Length of the Hello PDU, and the Neighbor Extended Local Circuit ID in four octets.

The three-way state values are 0 for Up, 1 for Initializing and 2 for Down. The Extended Local Circuit ID is a unique ID assigned to this circuit when it is created by the Intermediate System. The Neighbor System ID is the System ID of the neighbouring Intermediate System if it is known, and the Neighbor Extended Local Circuit ID is the Extended Local Circuit ID of the other end of the point-to-point adjacency if it is known.

Any system that supports this mechanism SHALL include the option in its point-to-point Hello packets, and any system that does not understand the option SHALL ignore it and SHALL NOT include it in its own Hello packets. A system that supports the mechanism MUST include the Adjacency Three-Way State field in this option; the other fields SHOULD be included as the procedures below explain.
sections.plainLanguage: The new information travels in a separate option added to the hello packet, with type 240. The option carries the three-way state in one byte, a four byte circuit ID chosen by the sending router, and the neighbour's system ID and circuit ID as it reported them.

sections.title: The Handshake Procedure
sections.content:
The new procedure is added to the IS-IS point-to-point Hello state machine after the PDU acceptance tests have been performed.

On receiving a Hello, a system sets the state it will report in the option to Down. On sending a Hello, the system includes the option, reports the current three-way state of the adjacency with its neighbour on the link, and reports Down if no adjacency exists. The Extended Local Circuit ID field holds a value assigned by the system when the circuit is created, which SHALL be unique among all the circuits of that Intermediate System; the value is not necessarily related to the one carried in the Local Circuit ID field. If the system ID and extended circuit ID of the neighbour are known, that is, in state Initializing or Up, the neighbour's system ID and extended circuit ID are reported back.

When a received Hello carries no option, the link is assumed to be functional in both directions and the existing procedures are followed. If the option is present but contains an invalid Adjacency Three-Way State, the PDU SHALL be discarded and no further action taken. If the option is present with a valid state, the Neighbor System ID and Neighbor Extended Local Circuit ID fields, if present, are examined. If the Neighbor System ID does not match the local system's ID, or the Neighbor Extended Local Circuit ID does not match the local system's extended circuit ID, the PDU SHALL be discarded.

The three-way state table then decides what happens, using the current three-way state and the state received in the option. The rows of the table are the local state and the columns the received state. From Down, receiving Down gives Initialize, receiving Initializing gives Up, and receiving Up gives Down. From Initializing, receiving Down gives Initialize, and receiving Initializing or Up gives Up. From Up, receiving Down gives Initialize, and receiving Initializing or Up gives Accept.

If the new action is Down, an adjacencyStateChange(Down) event is generated with the reason "Neighbor restarted" and the adjacency is deleted. If it is Initialize, no event is generated and the three-way state is set to Initializing. If it is Up, an adjacencyStateChange(Up) event is generated. The procedure works properly if neither the local nor the received state field is ever included, which gives backward compatibility to an earlier version of this option.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router sends a hello it always includes the option, reporting its own state and what it last heard from the neighbour. When it receives one, it checks that the neighbour really heard it: if the neighbour's system ID or circuit ID does not match what was sent, the packet is dropped. A small table then says what the new state should be.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document raises no new security issues for IS-IS. IS-IS security may be used to secure the IS-IS messages discussed here, as described in RFC 5304.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds nothing new to the security of IS-IS. The existing IS-IS authentication can protect these messages.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3373
sections.content: This document is a minor edit of RFC 3373 with the intent of advancing it from Informational to Standards Track. It also updates the ISO 10589 reference to refer to the current "2002" version.
sections.plainLanguage: The text is nearly the same as the earlier version of this extension, which was an Informational document. The main change is that it is now on the standards track, and the reference to the IS-IS standard points at the 2002 edition.

viz.caption: THE THREE FAILURE MODES THE EXTENSION FIXES

cells: The link comes back up, or a system restarts, and the CSNP is lost
The link state databases do not synchronize for a full LSP refresh period, up to 18 hours
The link fails in one direction only
Only one system notices; with two parallel links SPF still calculates paths and traffic goes down the failed direction
Interconnectivity changes without a link-layer-down condition
A system may receive packets meant for another system and think it has an adjacency it does not have

items.title: Down
items.text: The starting state. No Hello packet carrying the three-way handshake option has been received on this circuit.

items.title: Initializing
items.text: A Hello with the three-way option has been received from the neighbour, but it is not known whether the neighbour is receiving ours.

items.title: Up
items.text: The system knows that the neighbour is receiving its Hello packets.
